app/public/masters/stats.json (329,379 games, both players 2500+; first move e4 142,147, d4 117,599) [V]

steps.text: Every game record, chess book and coach talks in square names. Without them you cannot write down your own game, look up an opening, or ask a coach what to play on a given move. Learn the 64 names once and all of that opens up. By the end of this lesson you will read a short game record like the one on the next board.

steps.caption: A game record is a list of moves, each written with the square it lands on. This one says: e4, e5, Nf3. You cannot read it yet. By the end of the lesson you will, so watch what happens on the board.

line.say: The first entry, e4: a pawn lands on e4.
The second entry, e5: Black's pawn answers on e5.
The third entry, Nf3: a knight lands on f3.

steps.text: You just tapped the white king. The board is a grid of **64 squares**: 8 columns and 8 rows. Every square has its own name, like a street address, so two players can talk about the same square without pointing. Next you will see how a name is built from two parts, a letter and a number.

steps.caption: The white rook (the castle-shaped piece) climbs from the bottom row. A column of squares is called a **file**. Watch which part of each square's name stays the same.

line.say: The rook slides up its column. It now stands on d3.
Black's king steps aside. Ignore it and keep watching the rook.
Higher again, still in the same column: d6. The letter has not changed.

steps.caption: Now the rook slides sideways along a row. A row of squares is called a **rank**. Which part of the name stays the same this time?

line.say: Sliding sideways along the row: c4.
Black's king steps aside again.
Further along, still in the same row: f4. The number has not changed.

steps.text: Here is the pattern. A **file** is a column, named with a letter from **a** to **h**, counted from White's left. A **rank** is a row, numbered **1** to **8**, counted up from White's side. A square's name is its file letter first, then its rank number: d3 is file d, rank 3.

Why a letter and a number? [I] Two different kinds of symbol cannot be mixed up. In f5 the letter must name the column and the number the row, so nobody has to say which is which. This is my inference, not a sourced history.

steps.caption: Worked example: find f5. Run a finger up the f-file from the bottom (the vertical arrow) and along rank 5 from the left edge (the horizontal arrow). The two meet on f5, where the knight stands. Letter first, then number.
The four corners: the white rooks start on a1 and h1, the black rooks on a8 and h8. The white king starts on e1, facing the black king on e8.
Watch a pawn travel from e2 to e4. The letter stays, the number grows: it moves up the e-file.

line.say: The pawn leaves e2 and lands on e4, two rows up the same column.
Black's pawn mirrors it, from e7 to e5. Every square keeps its name.

steps.caption: Check your board with the colours. a1 is a dark square. Seen from White's side, the light square is in the bottom-right corner (h1), and from Black's side it is in the corner on Black's right (a8). Dark in your right-hand corner means the board is the wrong way round.

A **diagonal** is a line of same-coloured squares touching at their corners. The bishop on a1 sits on the long diagonal, which runs from a1 to h8 through b2, c3, d4, e5, f6 and g7. Name a diagonal by its end squares.

line.say: The bishop slides along the diagonal to d4. Both letter and number went up by three.
Black's king steps aside.
On to h8. Along a diagonal the letter and the number change together.

steps.caption: Some squares give a piece more room. A king steps one square in any direction. In the corner it has only three squares to go to. One step away, on b2, it has eight.

line.say: One step from the corner to b2, and the king already has eight squares to choose from.

steps.caption: The same king on e4, in the middle of the board, now has eight squares to go to. Pieces in the middle reach more of the board.

steps.text: The squares d4, e4, d5 and e5 are the **centre**. Znosko-Borovsky counted the squares a piece reaches from each square of an empty board, as a rough guide, not a law. A king reaches 3 squares from a1 and 8 from e4; a knight 2 and 8; a rook 14 from either. Of 329,379 games between players rated 2500+, 79 percent began with a pawn to e4 or d4.

steps.title: Same board, other side
steps.prompt: Predict first: the next two exercises show the same position, first from White's side and then turned around so you see it from Black's side. Will the name of the rook's square change?

steps.caption: Here is the answer to that prediction. The board is turned: you see it from Black's side, so Black's pieces are at the bottom. The white rook has not moved. It still stands on a1, now at the top right of your view. The names belong to the board, not to the picture.

steps.text: **Rule of thumb:** rank 1 is White's home row and rank 8 is Black's, whichever way the board is turned. If letters and numbers show on the board's edge, read them. If not, find White's home row first. [I] A likely slip is to copy the picture as White would: the rook you just saw would then be misread as h8.

steps.caption: Letter first, number second. The knight is on b3 and the bishop on c2. Swap the parts of a name and you land somewhere else: b3 is not 3b, and it is not c2 either.

steps.text: Three slips to watch for. [I] These come from my reading of how beginners go wrong, not from a study I checked. One: swapping the two parts, so b3 becomes c2. Two: counting ranks from the side you are looking from instead of from White's side. Three: mixing up file and rank, a column and a row.

steps.caption: Now the same names in written form. Pawn moves are only a square. Other pieces start with a capital letter. Step through and read each move as it is played. These moves are only here to practise reading notation (the Two Knights Defence, which you will meet later).

line.say: A pawn move is written as just the square it lands on: e4.
Black answers the same way: e5.
The knight is N, because K is taken by the king: Nf3.
Black's knight jumps out the same way: Nc6.
The bishop is B, so this move is Bc4.
The other black knight comes out: Nf6.
The knight goes to g5: Ng5.
Black's d-pawn steps forward: d5.
A pawn that captures starts with its file letter, then x: exd5.
A piece that captures puts x before the square: Nxd5.

steps.text: To write a move, use the piece's letter and the square it lands on: **K** king, **Q** queen, **R** rook, **B** bishop, **N** knight. A pawn has no letter, only the square, like e4. A capture adds an **x**, so Nxd5 is a knight capturing on d5. A pawn capture starts with the pawn's file letter, like exd5.

steps.caption: Castling has its own marks. The king hops two squares toward a rook and the rook jumps over it. Short castling is written O-O and long castling O-O-O. The lessons on castling come later; here you only need to read the symbol.

line.say: White castles short, toward the h-file rook: O-O.
Black castles long, toward the a-file rook: O-O-O.

steps.caption: A plus sign after a move means the king is attacked: check. The rook goes to a8 and attacks the black king along rank 8, so the move is Ra8+. The king must now escape.

line.say: Ra8+: the plus sign says the king is in check.
The king steps off the rank, to e7.

steps.caption: A hash sign means checkmate: the king is attacked and cannot escape. Here the rook's move to a8 attacks the king along rank 8, and the three black pawns block every square in front of it. Written Ra8#.

line.say: Ra8#: the game is over. The king cannot move away, block, or capture.

steps.caption: When a pawn reaches the far rank it is promoted, usually to a queen. The mark is an equals sign and the new piece's letter. Here the pawn lands on a8 and becomes a queen, which also gives check from a8: a8=Q+.

line.say: a8=Q+: the pawn becomes a queen and attacks the king along the rank.

steps.caption: Two knights can reach d7. Which one moves? The letter after the piece says where it comes from. The knight from the b-file is Nbd7. The other would be Nfd7. If both are on the same file, the rank number is used instead.

line.say: Nbd7: N for knight, b for the file it leaves from, d7 for where it lands.

steps.text: Marks to keep: **O-O** and **O-O-O** are short and long castling, **+** is check, **#** is checkmate, **=** and a piece letter is promotion, and an extra file letter after the piece says which of two pieces moved. You will meet each of them again in the lessons on castling, check and promotion.

steps.prompt: A friend sees a1 on a board turned to Black's side and says it must be h8. In your own words, tell them what to do and why. Write it as if you were teaching them.

fields.label: What I would tell my friend:

steps.text: **A model answer, to compare with yours.** Square names belong to the board, not to the picture. Find White's home row, rank 1, and White's left side, the a-file. From Black's side those are the top row and the right-hand edge, so a1 sits in the top right corner. To read a written move, take the piece's letter and the square it lands on.

steps.prompt: Which kind of square was slowest for you: a far corner, the middle, or a turned board? What will you check first next time? Rate how sure you are of naming any square without counting. (low / medium / high)
